whyChoose.title: What to Know Before You Pursue a Claim

items.title: Strict Filing Deadlines
items.desc: Under MICRA, you generally have one year from when you discovered the injury, and no more than three years from the date of the injury, to file. Missing that window can end a claim entirely, so early legal review matters.

items.title: 90-Day Notice Requirement
items.desc: California law requires sending a formal notice of intent to sue at least 90 days before filing a malpractice lawsuit. An attorney can help make sure this notice is prepared correctly and on time.

items.title: Expert Review Is Usually Required
items.desc: A qualified medical expert typically must confirm that the care fell below an accepted standard — a bad outcome alone doesn't establish malpractice. The attorneys in our network work with medical experts to evaluate whether a case has merit.

items.question: I had a bad outcome after surgery near Rolling Hills Estates — does that mean it was malpractice?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law recognizes that medicine involves risk, and a poor result alone doesn't prove negligence. An attorney would need to review your records and typically consult a medical expert to determine whether the care you received fell below an accepted standard.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a claim in California?
items.answer: Generally, you have one year from when you discovered the injury, and no more than three years from the date it occurred, to file a claim under MICRA. There's also a 90-day pre-suit notice requirement, so it's best not to wait to have your situation reviewed.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: Yes. California caps non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases, though that cap rises each year under current law. Economic damages, like medical bills and lost income, are generally not subject to this cap.
